query: For initially solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles exposed to the premelting and melting regime, the limited understanding of their thermal response prevents clear definition of their usable temperature range and behavior during high-temperature synthesis. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the onset and progression of their phase transition and why? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, relevant boundary conditions, supporting evidence from prior nanoparticle studies, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The thermal phase transition pathway in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles is kinetically modulated by the heating rate: slow heating (e.g., 1 K/min) enables sufficient atomic diffusion to form a metastable disordered precursor phase between approximately 800°C and 1000°C prior to complete melting, while fast heating (e.g., 10 K/min) bypasses this intermediate, leading to a direct solid-to-liquid transition.
generation.material_initial_state: Solid FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles with a narrow size distribution and homogeneous elemental composition.
generation.intervention: Subject identical nanoparticle samples to thermal treatments using two distinct heating rates—a slow rate of 1 K/min and a fast rate of 10 K/min—while monitoring the process via DSC and in situ TEM.
generation.conditions: Inert (Ar) atmosphere; temperature ramp from room temperature to above the complete melting point, comparing slow (1 K/min) versus fast (10 K/min) rates.
generation.structural_mediator: At slow heating, atomic diffusion permits the transient formation of a metastable disordered phase that serves as an intermediate precursor prior to full melting, a state that does not develop under rapid heating.
generation.mechanism: Sufficient time at intermediate temperatures under slow heating allows for atomic reordering into a metastable disordered state (expected between 800°C and 1000°C) that precedes melting; conversely, rapid heating kinetically suppresses this phase, resulting in a direct transition from solid to liquid.
generation.predicted_outcome: DSC curves obtained at 1 K/min will exhibit an extra thermal event (secondary peak or inflection) corresponding to the formation of a metastable disordered phase, which will be absent in DSC curves at 10 K/min; in situ TEM will visually capture distinct intermediate structural changes in the slow-heated samples.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles heated at an intermediate rate of about 5 K/min typically show a single melting endotherm with no evidence of a metastable intermediate phase.
generation.boundary: This phenomenon is expected for heating rates between 1 and 10 K/min and for nanoparticles with a controlled narrow size distribution; effects may not be observable in significantly larger particles or if heating is performed outside this range.
generation.uncertainty: The precise temperature range and lifetime of the metastable phase may vary with minor differences in particle size or experimental setup, and overlapping signals from size dispersion could obscure the effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Heat identical nanoparticle samples at 1 K/min and 10 K/min under strictly controlled conditions while recording high-resolution DSC traces and capturing real-time structural evolution with in situ TEM. Ensure particle size and composition are consistent across samples.
measurements: DSC to identify additional thermal events
In situ TEM to capture the emergence (or absence) of an intermediate disordered phase
XRD or diffraction analysis post-heating to assess phase differences
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the slow-heated sample does not display a reproducible additional thermal event or if no morphological intermediate is observed compared to the fast-heated sample, the hypothesis is falsified.

Upon completing the disorder-to-order transition, we found that the ultrasmall MPEI nanoparticles displayed excellent phase stability, as evidenced by in situ heating a quinary Pt(Fe0.7Co0.1Ni0.1Cu0.1) MPEI nanoparticle and simultaneously monitoring its phase evolution by STEM (Fig. 4D). The quinary MPEI nanoparticle synthesized by Joule heating displayed a fully ordered structure even after 13 min of additional heating at ~1100 K, as indicated by the (001) diffraction spot in the fast Fourier transform (FT) image. We then held the nanoparticle at ~1100 K for another 47 min and still did not observe a phase change, indicating the thermal stability of the MPEI nanoparticle. In contrast, the binary PtFe nanoparticles (~5 nm) at ~1100 K showed an ordered intermetallic structure (14 min) but gradually transformed to a disordered alloy (60 min), indicating the superior thermal stability of MPEIs compared to binary intermetallics (fig. papers.title: Microstructure and Thermal Analysis of Metastable Intermetallic Phases in High-Entropy Alloy CoCrFeMo0.85Ni.
papers.system: High-entropy alloy powder (CoCrFeMo0.85Ni), used as a proxy for complex HEA nanoparticles.
papers.approach: Thermal analysis via DTA/DSC combined with microstructural characterization (SEM/EDX) during controlled heating cycles.
papers.findings: Distinct thermal events were observed – an exothermal process near 800 °C indicating the onset of intermetallic phase formation (e.g., μ and σ phases) and an endothermic event around 1212 °C corresponding to phase dissolution. Subsequent cycles showed a solidus/liquidus window identified around 1320–1330 °C.
papers.mechanism: Phase transitions are driven by compositional modulations and the release/absorption of latent heat associated with phase formation and dissolution; nucleation of intermetallic phases is sensitive to thermal history and heating rate.

papers.title: Multi-principal elemental intermetallic nanoparticles synthesized via a disorder-to-order transition.
papers.system: Ultrasmall multi-principal element intermetallic nanoparticles (e.g., PtPdAuFeCoNiCuSn) synthesized via a controlled Joule heating process on carbon substrates.
papers.approach: Rapid Joule heating (55 ms) to form disordered HEA nanoparticles followed by a short reheating period (5 min) at ~1100 K to induce a disorder‐to‐order transformation; monitored using in situ STEM and Monte Carlo modeling.
papers.findings: The process yields nanoparticles that exhibit a fully ordered L10 structure after the controlled anneal at ~1100 K. The ordered phase remains stable upon prolonged heating, in contrast with binary systems that gradually disorder at extended times.
papers.mechanism: The transformation is driven by the significant decrease in formation enthalpy (ΔHf) and the resultant lowering of Gibbs free energy, which favors atomic reordering (disorder-to-order transition) under a narrow thermal window.

papers.title: Laser solid-phase synthesis of graphene shell-encapsulated high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
papers.system: High-entropy alloy nanoparticles (e.g., CrMnFeCoNi) produced on a graphene substrate via laser irradiation.
papers.approach: Laser-induced heating under controlled fluence and scanning rates to decompose metal salt precursors; real-time temperature measurements and thermal simulations to track heating/cooling profiles.
papers.findings: Despite reaching temperatures above the melting point, the nanoparticles remain on a similar length scale as prior to melting. This is attributed to the laser-induced high pressure causing molten beads to split into smaller droplets, followed by rapid quenching.
papers.mechanism: The interplay between high localized temperature and laser-induced pressure affects the molten phase dynamics, preventing agglomeration by splitting up the liquid droplets and rapidly quenching them to a nanoscale size.

papers.title: Continuous synthesis of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles by in-flight alloying of elemental metals.
papers.system: HEA nanoparticles synthesized from elemental metal vapors using a thermal plasma jet under different gas atmospheres (e.g., H2 vs He).
papers.approach: Use of thermal plasma for rapid heating/atomization of metal powders, with in-flight alloying and subsequent rapid cooling. Comparative study under different plasma gas conditions to elucidate nucleation and growth pathways.
papers.findings: Under hydrogen, nanoparticles predominantly form via the VLS (vapor-liquid-solid) mechanism, resulting in slightly amorphous states and larger size distributions due to liquid-phase coalescence. In helium, the VS (vapor-solid) mechanism prevails, leading to higher crystallinity and more uniform particle sizes.
papers.mechanism: Nanoparticle growth is controlled by the interplay between melting (liquid phase formation) and rapid quenching dynamics, where the gas environment dictates whether a VLS or VS mechanism is dominant, impacting phase homogeneity and size distribution.

directions.assessment: This direction posits that one or more elements (e.g., Cu, which has a lower melting point) preferentially segregate to the nanoparticle surface under heating. This lowers the local melting threshold and induces premelting from the surface inward. The approach directly targets the nanoscale interfacial energy and melting point depression issues. Prior nanoparticle laser‐synthesis studies (e.g., PMC11427457::web::015) support rapid surface‐enabled dynamics and it is experimentally feasible to compare passivated and non‐passivated nanoparticles.

This proposal focuses on the inherent size effects in nanoparticles. As the particle size decreases (increasing surface‐to‐volume ratio), the melting point is known to depress. A controlled size‐selection or sorting study can reveal the correlation between size and the onset of premelting. Laser ablation and colloidal synthesis studies have shown dramatic effects of size (e.g., PMC9064730::web::007), making this direction both feasible and directly relevant.

directions.direction: Kinetic modulation via thermal ramp rate
directions.assessment: This direction asserts that the heating rate (ramp rate) controls whether a metastable precursor or disorder‐to‐order intermediate state forms (as seen in some rapid Joule heating studies [PMC8797181::web::014]), delaying or advancing the phase transition onset. Experimentally varying the heating rate is straightforward and can yield direct information on the kinetic barrier governing phase transition, although transient intermediate phases might be subtle.

directions.direction: Surface energy modification by pre‐heating induced roughness
directions.type: Processing, surface treatment and microstructure control
directions.assessment: This approach hypothesizes that if the nanoparticle surface is roughened or contains defects (for example, via a mild pre‐annealing step), the increased surface energy will act as nucleation sites for melting. This can accelerate the phase transition onset. Although more challenging to quantify, prior studies have noted that laser‐induced pressures (PMC11427457::web::014) affect surface dynamics, making this a promising and testable direction.

This theoretical direction considers that the balance between local surface energy and bulk cohesive energy can lead to heterogeneous melting events inside the nanoparticle. While promising from a modelling perspective (see, e.g., PMC11576752::web::013::melting_simulation), experimental control may be more challenging. This approach is less direct than the others but still complementary.
